content: A clinical study by 'Merck' showed that the new pneumococcal vaccine Capvaxive elicits strong and effective immune responses in children and adolescents aged 2‑18 with chronic illnesses or immunodeficiency, outperforming the older PPSV23 vaccine. The study, which included participants up to 18 years old, demonstrated that Capvaxive covers a wide range of pneumococcal serotypes responsible for pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis—diseases that pose a serious threat to vulnerable populations. Safety data indicated no serious adverse events during the trial, supporting the likelihood of future regulatory approval. Researchers suggest that incorporating Capvaxive into national immunization programs could markedly reduce respiratory disease burden, lower mortality, and decrease hospital admissions, especially in communities lacking robust health systems or facing high rates of antibiotic‑resistant bacterial infections.

content: A new vaccine against 21 strains of pneumococcal disease is being developed in a joint international study. The study aims to provide greater protection for children against the common infection that causes pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis. According to 'News medical life science', the study led by the Murdoch Children's Research Institute (MCRI) in Australia is evaluating a promising vaccine that protects against 21 strains of pneumococcal disease, compared to the current 13 strains included in the national immunization program. The Melbourne branch of the randomized controlled trial will test 50 families with healthy two-month-old children who have not received routine vaccinations. Participants will receive four doses of the vaccine at two months, four and a half months, and 12-15 months, in addition to all recommended childhood vaccinations in the national immunization plan (NIP). The study aims to enroll over 1600 children from Australia, the United States, Puerto Rico, Honduras, South Korea, and Thailand to ensure the vaccine's safety and ability to induce protective antibody responses in young children. Participants will be followed up for up to 19 months and will undergo three blood tests. Pneumococcal disease can cause severe illnesses and death in children under two years old. In 2024, 602 cases of invasive pneumococcal disease were reported in Victoria, including 373 cases among children aged 0-4 years. content: The article discusses the upcoming upgrade of the pneumococcal vaccine in Taiwan, scheduled for 2026, to effectively address serotype replacement caused by widespread childhood vaccination. Since the introduction of the PCV13 vaccine for children ten years ago, there has been a significant reduction in severe pneumococcal infections, particularly among children, and a corresponding indirect protective effect observed in elderly populations. However, as seen in the U.S. experience, the widespread use of childhood vaccines has led to serotype replacement—where non-vaccine serotypes become more prevalent. To combat this, advanced countries such as the U.S., Canada, and EU nations have adopted PCV20 and PCV21 as priority vaccines for older adults and high-risk groups. In Taiwan, the Ministry of Health and Welfare’s Infectious Disease Prevention Advisory Committee, in a meeting held in September 2025, decided that individuals aged 19 to 64 with high-risk conditions who have completed a PCV13/15 and PPV23 series before age 65 may receive a booster dose of PCV20 or PCV21 within five years. The article emphasizes that increasing pneumococcal vaccination rates, especially among high-risk groups, is critical to maintaining public health protection.

title: Mycoplasma Testing Market Set to Grow at a 11.5% CAGR, Crossing the US$ 4.52 Billion Mark by 2032

Major players such as Lonza, Merck, Thermo Fisher and Roche are investing in rapid PCR and digital PCR technologies and forming partnerships with CROs/CMOs to strengthen their service‑based revenue models. title: U-led vaccine project seeks to counter federal inaction, misinformation
content: The University-led vaccine project aims to counter federal inaction and misinformation by synthesizing data on vaccine safety and effectiveness. The project will focus on older adults at high risk of infection-related hospitalizations and deaths, as well as the general population. A searchable website will be created to provide information on vaccine safety and effectiveness for different demographic groups. Researchers found strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of the nirsevimab vaccine in preventing RSV-related hospitalizations and complications in children, but no recent studies provided safety or effectiveness results for clesrovimab, a federally recommended antibody therapy.
